analysis.investment_thesis: Craftsman Automation has delivered an impressive 22.8% revenue CAGR over 8 years in Indian auto components, but the business is currently burdened by D/E of 1.09, ROE of just 9.4%, and a net profit decline from 337 Cr (FY24) to 201 Cr (FY25) despite revenues reaching 5,690 Cr. At 52.2x P/E with a 992 Cr capex programme driving -706 Cr free cash flow, the current risk-reward does not excite me.
key_strengths: 8-year revenue CAGR of 22.8% to 5,690 Cr demonstrates real operational capability and customer trust in precision engineering
Diversified across powertrain, aluminium die-casting, and industrial/warehousing segments — reducing single-sector dependency
Strong institutional validation: FII 15.19% + DII 28.29% = 43.5% institutional holding signals recognized quality
key_risks: D/E of 1.09 with borrowings jumping from 1,755 to 3,311 Cr in FY25 — aggressive leverage in a cyclical auto components sector is dangerous
ROE of 9.41% and ROCE of 11.7% are both below my 15% minimum threshold — returns on incremental capital are not compelling
Finance cost has grown to 217 Cr (FY25) and is expanding rapidly — rising interest burden will suppress earnings even as revenue grows
red_flags: Net profit fell from 337 Cr (FY24) to 201 Cr (FY25) — a 40% decline — despite a 28% revenue jump to 5,690 Cr, signalling poor incremental profitability
Free cash flow of -706 Cr in FY25 and capex of 992 Cr — balance sheet stretched at the worst point in the earnings cycle
Total assets near-doubled from 4,706 to 8,266 Cr in one year — likely a large acquisition; integration/valuation risk is unclear
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Craftsman's revenue growth story is genuinely impressive — from 1,102 Cr in 2017 to 5,690 Cr in 2025 is outstanding execution. The Coimbatore promoter has built a real business. But I am not comfortable buying at 52x P/E when profits are falling, debt has surged to D/E of 1.09, and the company is burning 706 Cr of free cash flow. The massive capex cycle (992 Cr in FY25 alone) and the near-doubling of total assets suggest either a transformative acquisition or an aggressive greenfield expansion — neither of which justifies current valuation when the business earns only 9.4% ROE.

The auto components sector has genuine India tailwinds — rising vehicle production, EV content per vehicle, Make in India manufacturing push. Craftsman could be a long-term winner. But I want to see the capex convert to earnings: ROE must recover above 15%, debt must start declining, and profits must show a clear uptrend before I commit capital. This is a watchlist candidate, not a buy at current prices and capital structure.
